title: Ventricular predominance in biventricular arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy: Should new subtype criteria be recognized?
case_prompt: A 68-year-old man was admitted after chest discomfort, palpitations, and light-headedness followed by a syncopal episode. He had a history of progressive exercise intolerance, heart failure, and ventricular tachycardia treated with cardioversion one year earlier. Current medications were bisoprolol, spironolactone, aspirin, and amiodarone. Family history was unremarkable. On arrival, heart rate was 66 bpm, blood pressure 103/64 mmHg, oxygen saturation 98% on room air, and respiratory rate 12/min. Laboratory studies were normal except for mild hyponatremia (Na+ 134 mEq/L). Continuous monitoring captured a sustained monomorphic ventricular tachycardia, which was pharmacologically cardioverted to sinus rhythm. The post-conversion ECG showed low QRS voltages in the limb leads and T-wave inversions in leads V4–V6. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed an LVEF of 30%, RV systolic dysfunction (TAPSE 17 mm; S’ 5.2 cm/s; RV fractional area change 27%), biatrial enlargement, and biventricular global hypokinesia. Coronary CT angiography showed no atherosclerotic plaques (CAD-RADS 0). Cardiac MRI demonstrated biventricular enlargement (LVEF 34%, RVEF 27%), septal dyssynchrony, a linear hypointense signal in the basal septum on T2 imaging, and extensive subepicardial ring-pattern late gadolinium enhancement of the left ventricular free wall and septum with irregular morphology of the RV free wall.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Myopericarditis — “In the early stage, myopericarditis, sarcoidosis, and other inflammatory diseases need to be ruled out.”  
2. Sarcoidosis — “Neither of these criteria was present in our patient.”  
3. Ischemic cardiomyopathy — “Cardiovascular computed tomography ruled out atherosclerotic plaques (CAD-RADS 0).”  
4. Non-ischemic dilated cardiomyopathy — “Most DCM patients do not exhibit LGE, but in those who do, it most often occurs in a linear pattern in the mid-wall of the septum... DCM does not involve the RV, while LDAC is more often associated with malignant ventricular arrhythmias.”  
5. RV outflow tract tachycardia — “In patients with suspected ARVC, conditions associated with primary arrhythmias, such as RV outflow tract tachycardia, and Brugada syndrome, must be investigated.”  
6. Brugada syndrome — “However, these patients do not have RV systolic dysfunction or global dilatation.”  
7. Structural heart diseases (congenital defects, pulmonary hypertension, athlete’s heart) — “Other diagnoses that should be considered are structural diseases, such as other congenital heart diseases (left to right shunt, Uhl's anomaly and Ebstein’s anomaly), pulmonary artery hypertension, and athlete’s heart.”  
8. RV infarction — “RV infarction should also be considered; however, it is associated with a specific vascular territory and lacks the characteristic features of ACM... LGE in RV infarction typically begins at the subendocardial level, in contrast to ARVC...”  
9. Neuromuscular cardiomyopathies, congenital ventricular aneurysms, and Chagas’ heart disease — “Moreover, other diagnosis that should be considered are neuromuscular cardiomyopathies (muscular dystrophies and myofibrillar myopathies), myocarditis, sarcoidosis, congenital ventricular aneurysms, and even Chagas’ heart disease.”
